question: Why is validity on a frame a second-order condition, when truth at a world in a model is not?
options: It quantifies over every assignment of truth values to atoms, that is, over all sets of worlds
It quantifies over every frame at once, and frames are themselves relational structures
The box is a quantifier over accessible worlds, and nesting boxes raises the order each time
It requires following chains of accessible worlds of every length, which no single formula can
explanation: A frame fixes worlds and relation but not the assignment, so validity there says "for every assignment", a quantification over subsets of the set of worlds. The box quantifies over worlds, which is first-order, however deeply it is nested.

question: A formula true at every world of one particular model built on a frame is valid on that frame.
options: True
False
explanation: Validity on a frame requires truth at every world under every assignment, so one model is one assignment among many. $\Box \varphi \rightarrow \varphi$ is true throughout any model making $\varphi$ true everywhere, even on a frame where it is not valid.

question: In a frame where some world $w$ does not see itself, which assignment falsifies $\Box \varphi \rightarrow \varphi$ at $w$?
options: Make $\varphi$ true at $w$ and nowhere else
Make $\varphi$ false at every world, so that both sides of the conditional fail at $w$
Make $\varphi$ true at every world except $w$
Make $\varphi$ true at every world, so that $\Box \varphi$ is certain to hold at $w$
explanation: Every world $w$ sees then satisfies $\varphi$, so $\Box \varphi$ holds at $w$, while $\varphi$ fails there. This is the general pattern: make the atom true exactly where the frame condition would have required it, and the missing link shows up as a counterexample.

question: A frame has two worlds, $w$ and $v$; $w$ sees $v$, and nothing else is related. Which of these axioms is valid on it?
options: $\Box \varphi \rightarrow \varphi$
$\Box \varphi \rightarrow \Diamond \varphi$, since $w$ sees a world and so does every other
$\varphi \rightarrow \Box \Diamond \varphi$, since the only link runs in a single direction
$\Box \varphi \rightarrow \Box \Box \varphi$
explanation: There is no two-step path at all, so the frame is trivially transitive and axiom 4 holds. It is not reflexive, it is not serial because $v$ sees nothing, and it is not symmetric because $v$ does not see $w$, so T, D and B all fail.

question: Why does no first-order condition on frames correspond to the Löb axiom?
options: Because the Löb axiom lies outside the Sahlqvist class
By compactness, a first-order theory of "no infinite ascending chain" would have a model with one
Because its frames must be irreflexive, and irreflexivity cannot be stated in first-order terms
Because transitivity, which its frames also need, is itself not a first-order condition
explanation: Add constants and sentences saying each sees the next; every finite part has a model among the intended frames, so compactness yields one with an infinite chain. Falling outside the Sahlqvist class only withdraws a guarantee, and irreflexivity and transitivity are both first-order.

question: A modal formula falls outside Sahlqvist's syntactic class. What follows?
options: Nothing definite: Sahlqvist's theorem then offers no guarantee either way
It corresponds to no first-order condition on frames, since Sahlqvist's class contains them all
It cannot be canonical, since canonicity is proved only for Sahlqvist formulas
It is valid on no frame at all
explanation: The theorem gives a sufficient condition: Sahlqvist formulas have computable first-order correspondents and are canonical. Formulas outside the class may or may not have either property; the Löb axiom happens to have neither, but it is valid on plenty of frames.

question: A normal modal logic is shown to be canonical. What follows directly?
options: Its axioms are defined by first-order conditions on the accessibility relation
Every one of its axioms is a Sahlqvist formula
It is complete with respect to the class of frames its axioms define
It is decidable, since its canonical frame can be searched for countermodels
explanation: The canonical frame validates the axioms, so it belongs to the class they define, and any non-theorem fails in the canonical model; hence completeness, uniformly. Canonicity and first-order definability are independent, and Sahlqvist formulas are only one source of canonical logics.

question: Every canonical modal logic is defined by some first-order condition on frames.
options: True
False
explanation: Canonicity and first-order definability are independent: there are canonical logics defined by no first-order condition, and first-order conditions defining no canonical logic. Sahlqvist formulas have both properties, which is why they are easily confused.

question: The objection says correspondence results are mere computations within a definition. On the reply, what goes beyond that?
options: The individual translations, such as axiom 4 into transitivity, which had to be discovered
The fact that every modal formula turns out to have some first-order correspondent
The proof that frame validity is first-order after all, once the box is unpacked
General theorems, such as Sahlqvist's, that could have gone otherwise and had to be proved
explanation: The reply grants that individual translations follow from the definitions, as every theorem does, and points to the general results: a syntactic class always yields first-order conditions, some modally definable classes are not first-order, and modal definability has an exact characterisation. Not every formula has a first-order correspondent, as the Löb axiom shows.
